prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and topological insulators, and the first experimental observation of the quantum spin Hall state

statement.case_for: Topological insulators supply a simple, general and rigorous organising principle: a bulk Z2 invariant that dictates protected boundary states, independent of microscopic detail. That is the kind of universal mechanism that carries across disciplines, and it did: the idea spread to photonics, cold atoms, acoustics and mechanics. The Kane-Mele proposal was followed by decisive, independently confirmed experiments (HgTe quantum wells in 2007, then Bi-Sb and Bi2Se3 by ARPES in 2008-09), so theory and experiment reinforce each other cleanly. The field is now fifteen to twenty years old, with a stable interpretation, so the recognition is mature and arguably overdue. After rereading colleagues' ballots I move Mele back into my slate. Kane and Mele wrote the same founding papers, and a prize that credits the Z2 theory should not split them. That leaves Molenkamp as the experimental anchor, because the quantum spin Hall observation is the unambiguous experimental discovery that turned a prediction into a field.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. Any three-person slate omits defensible claimants: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang made the HgTe proposal that the 2007 experiment tested (Zhang is not among the credited names and is deceased), Fu and Kane's 3D theory, Moore and Balents, and Hasan, whose group made the first 3D topological insulator observations. Dropping Hasan to keep Kane, Mele and Molenkamp is a real cost, and a physicist who cares about who identified the mechanism first should say so. A second concern is that the 2016 prize on topological phase transitions covers neighbouring ground, so the committee may see this as incremental. The practical consequences are also still modest compared with, for example, clocks or circuit QED.

responses.point: Kroll ranks topological insulators only fifth, as conceptually important but less measurement-oriented, and he prefers Kane, Mele and Molenkamp as the slate while leaving Hasan out. His first choice is optical lattice clocks (B001).
responses.response: I agree with his three names and have moved to them. I do not accept that the topic is less of a measurement achievement: HgTe edge conductance of 2e^2/h and the ARPES Dirac cones are precise, quantitative confirmations of a bulk-boundary correspondence. I do think his criterion, that progress is limited by how well we can measure, fits lattice clocks well and I treat B001 as a strong competitor. Where we differ is that I give more weight to an organising concept that changed how materials are searched, and the clocks, to my mind, are a superb instrument whose conceptual novelty beyond the magic-wavelength idea is smaller.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first, as the clearest case of experiment surprising theory, with a quantitative continuum band-structure prediction, and he ranks topological insulators second.
responses.response: I share his admiration of the Bistritzer-MacDonald magic angle: a simple analytical result confirmed experimentally is what I like best. My disagreement is about maturity. The pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is unsettled, sample dependence is large, and only eight years have passed, whereas the topological insulator results have been reproduced across transport, ARPES and STM and have stood for fifteen years or more. I would also ask him how he would allocate between Bistritzer, Andrei and Cao-type experimental credit; his own slate takes Andrei and omits Bistritzer, which seems to reverse the theory priority. Unless that is resolved I keep B013 as my first alternative rather than the lead.

responses.point: Lindroth puts optical lattice clocks first, valuing the simple magic-wavelength trick that removes the light shift, the 1e-18 uncertainties, and the clean two-person configuration of Katori and Ye, with a natural continuation from the 2005 comb prize.
responses.response: I take the clean two-name attribution seriously, since that is a real advantage over my own slate, where the cut to three is painful. I also agree the magic-wavelength idea is exactly a simple mechanism with large consequences. My reservation is that the 2005 prize and the 2012 ion work already honoured much of the precision-timekeeping lineage, so the marginal conceptual step is the lattice trick plus engineering to 1e-18. Topological insulators opened a new class of matter rather than improving an existing measurement. I would not oppose B001, but I would want her to say what decisive physical discovery it adds beyond improved accuracy, which the redefinition of the second has not yet delivered.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first as a clean, fully controllable demonstration of basic quantum physics that became the dominant platform for superconducting processors, and he sees it as complementary to last year's prize.
responses.response: I accept that the Blais-Wallraff-Schoelkopf trio is a sensible theory plus experiment configuration. But I am not persuaded that it is complementary rather than adjacent to the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits: both are about superconducting circuits as quantum objects, and the credit overlaps with Devoret, Girvin and Nakamura, none of whom are in the credited names. A second prize in the same platform within a year would, in my view, look like fatigue. I also note that its main value, as a computing architecture, is partly engineering.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the IceCube neutrino discovery first because it opened a new window on the cosmos through nature's clues rather than theory, and he sees the single-laureate configuration with Halzen as clean.
responses.response: The discovery is solid and I find the Galactic plane and TXS 0506+056 evidence persuasive. My doubt is attribution: a single laureate for a collaboration of hundreds, with AMANDA and DUMAND predecessors and the analysts who found the first events, seems to me neither clean nor easy to defend, and the prize rules need a person. I would like him to explain why Halzen alone, rather than a configuration including later leaders, is the right reading. In contrast, topological insulators have a clear theory-experiment pairing even if the cut is painful.

uncertainties: Whether to credit Hasan instead of Mele, or to restructure so that 3D topological insulators are recognised; I have not settled how to weigh theory priority against the first 3D observation.
How the committee should treat the omission of Zhang, Bernevig and Hughes, whose HgTe proposal motivated the 2007 experiment, and Fu, Moore and Balents for the 3D theory.
Whether the 2016 prize on topological phases makes the committee regard this as too close to prior recognition.
I rely on my own memory of the history and have not verified dates or priority claims.
Whether optical lattice clocks (B001) deserve to lead given the strong cross-committee support; I do not yet know the weight colleagues put on precision measurement against a conceptual advance.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. I have no known collaboration with any credited name for the shortlisted candidates. I share the Gothenburg physics environment with Johansson and Olsson (Chalmers), which is institutional only, and neither a candidate nor a nominee is connected to Gothenburg.
